title: Visiting Slate’s first showroom as its $25,000 electric truck nears production
gist: Slate opened its first showroom in a former Chicago Tesla store and is holding its bare-bones electric pickup at $24,950, with first trucks going to investors and employees by year-end and early orderers in early 2027. Only a hand-built older prototype was on display, the Warsaw, Indiana line is still doing prototype runs, and Bangeman flags production quality as the key risk, alongside a race against Ford's sub-$30,000 Fathom.

themes.theme: Pricing, timing, and the affordable EV pickup gap

insights.claim: Slate is staying with its $24,950 price for the Slate Truck, a bare-bones electric pickup with plastic panels, manual window winders, and a projected 205-mile range.
insights.speaker: Eric Bangeman
insights.so_what: Holding price amid cost pressure is a test of Slate's unit economics and of its claim to be the low-cost EV leader.

insights.claim: Slate will ship some trucks by year-end to investors and employees, with early orderers receiving Slate Trucks in early 2027.
insights.speaker: Eric Bangeman
insights.so_what: Customer deliveries are effectively in 2027, so watch for slippage.
insights.quote: “Those will go to investors and employees, with early-orderers receiving their Slate Trucks in early 2027.
insights.locator: Purdy told me that Slate is staying

insights.claim: Bangeman argues there is no shortage of electric pickups but a shortage of affordable ones, so at about $25,000 the Slate undercuts the Rivian R1T, Cybertruck, Silverado EV, and every shipping battery-electric truck, and could be a breakout hit, especially if it beats Ford's sub-$30,000 Fathom to market.
insights.speaker: Eric Bangeman
insights.so_what: Low-cost EV pickups are a race to market between Slate and Ford, with first-mover timing as the key variable.
insights.quote: there is no shortage of electrified pickup trucks on the market, there is a shortage of affordable ones
insights.locator: Monday morning is not exactly prime time

insights.claim: The only Slate Truck in the showroom was a hand-built older prototype with a black wrap, and the Warsaw, Indiana assembly line is still doing prototyping runs with production hoped for 'soon'.
insights.speaker: Eric Bangeman
insights.so_what: Slate is still pre-production less than three months before its promised deliveries, which is a high execution risk.
insights.locator: The exterior passed the eye test

insights.claim: Bangeman's key risk is consistent build quality at scale (panel gaps, watertight seals, door-to-fender transitions, frunk alignment), citing Tesla's early Model Y defects and Cybertruck panel-gap problems as precedent.
insights.speaker: Eric Bangeman
insights.so_what: Early quality problems at a new automaker can damage the brand and slow the ramp, so watch first-delivery reviews.
insights.quote: no one knows if the Slate Trucks delivered to customers will live up to the promise of the carefully hand-built prototypes

insights.claim: Even on the display prototype, the seatback recline lever didn't work, though panels looked well fitted and the door closed with a solid thunk.
insights.speaker: Eric Bangeman
insights.so_what: This is a small sign that the build still isn't finished.

insights.claim: Slate opened its first showroom on October 15 in a former Tesla store in Chicago's Fulton Market, staffed partly by former Tesla employees, taking $300 deposits; it will not give sales numbers but calls the response 'incredible'.
insights.speaker: Eric Bangeman
insights.so_what: Demand evidence is anecdotal and refundable deposits are a weak signal, so look for conversion data.
insights.quote: “We’re really happy with the number of [$300] deposits we’ve gotten since we opened,”
insights.locator: The showroom has been open since October 15

insights.claim: Most Slate customers are choosing the truck configuration over the Squareback and Fastback SUV kits and then customizing it, according to the customer experience manager.
insights.speaker: Eric Bangeman
insights.so_what: Revenue from customization may matter more than the SUV kits for margins.
insights.quote: “Most customers are going with the truck configuration,”
insights.locator: Beyond the default Blank Slate body style

insights.claim: Slate is using RepairPal's network of 4,000 shops for service, some able to work on high-voltage systems, while owners can replace plastic body panels themselves; replacement part pricing isn't finalized.
insights.speaker: Eric Bangeman
insights.so_what: An asset-light service model lowers capex, but unknown parts pricing leaves total cost of ownership unclear.
insights.locator: For service, Slate will be using RepairPal
